teachingNote:
Orange mushroom, hymenium running down the stem, autumn woods. Almost everything a beginner reaches for here is shared by all three species, which is why this set is the first one.

What does not separate them: all three run their spore-bearing surface down the stem, so 'decurrent' proves nothing. All three cut solid and pale, and none of the three changes colour when sliced, so bruising is silent. All three have a plain stem base, so digging it up teaches you nothing — which is worth learning before you meet an Amanita, where digging it up is the whole game.

Growth habit is the trap inside the trap. Dense clustering is *suggestive* of the jack-o'-lantern and chanterelles rarely do it, but both chanterelles here are recorded as growing in small or loose clusters, and the sources give a tendency rather than a rule. A forager who reasons 'it's clustered, so it's a jack-o'-lantern' — or worse, 'it isn't tightly clustered, so it's a chanterelle' — is reasoning from a character that cannot carry the weight. It sits in redHerrings and CI holds it there.

What does separate them: the Appalachian chanterelle has well-developed false gills with cross-veins; the smooth chanterelle has a hymenium that is smooth to shallowly wrinkled; the jack-o'-lantern has true gills, thin and crowded and separable. Both chanterelles are mycorrhizal from soil and smell strongly of apricot; the jack-o'-lantern grows from hardwood and smells of nothing.

The spore print is the surprise, and it fails in exactly the wrong place. The smooth chanterelle drops a pale pinkish yellow print, which separates it from everything else in this set. The Appalachian chanterelle drops a white-to-creamy print — and so, sometimes, does the jack-o'-lantern, whose print runs white to creamy to pale yellow. So the one pairing the print cannot resolve is the dull orange chanterelle against the jack-o'-lantern: the pair a forager is most likely to be holding, and the pair where being wrong costs the most. The technique that saves you from a destroying angel is silent on the question that actually matters here.

It only works at all on dark paper. Cream, pale yellow and pale pinkish yellow are one colour on white paper; put the cap half on white and half on black and they separate. A character can be decisive, irrelevant, and conditional on your technique all at once.

The smooth chanterelle is here to break the rule before it hardens. A player who has learned 'ridges good, gills bad' meets a chanterelle with neither and has to fall back on substrate and odor. That is the transferable skill: characters are evidence, not rules. Ask it for its gill edges and it has none — 'not-applicable' is an answer, and it is the reason gill edge is not a discriminator in this set.

The substrate check has a trap in it. Jack-o'-lanterns fruit from buried roots, so a cluster can appear to rise straight out of bare ground. Nothing about the way it grows will rescue you there. The underside and the smell will: true gills and no apricot.

Odor is the most fragile of the four and the game treats it that way — rain takes it out, and an individual with weathering above 0.4 will not give it up at all.
